questions.prompt: A prospect gives you a one-word answer after your opening question. Your instinct is to:

options.text: Ask another question straight away to keep momentum
Offer more detail about your product to fill the gap
Acknowledge what they said and bridge to your next point
Reflect their word back to them as a question
Name the flatness in their tone and hold the silence

questions.prompt: Mid-meeting, a prospect says: "We tried something like this before and it didn't work." You:

options.text: Jump to reassurance: "This time will be different, I promise."
Apologise for their past experience and offer better terms to smooth things over
Ask a simple follow-up: "Can you tell me what happened?"
Reflect it back: "Didn't work?" and hold the silence to see what surfaces
Name the feeling underneath it: "That experience left you cautious about trying again."

questions.prompt: There is a 7-second pause after you ask a prospect what's holding the decision up. You:

options.text: Fill the silence with another angle on your pitch
Repeat the question in slightly different words
Wait it out and let them arrive at their own answer
Offer a guess at what might be holding them up, to give them a starting point
Name the pause itself: "That took a moment. What were you weighing up?"

questions.prompt: A prospect says "let me think about it" at the end of a strong meeting. Your read is:

options.text: They're being polite and the answer is probably no
They genuinely need time to weigh it up, no need to probe further
There's an unspoken concern they haven't raised yet
Someone else holds influence over this and hasn't been named
Name it directly: "When people say that, there's usually something specific behind it. What is it for you?"

questions.prompt: Mid-pitch, a prospect crosses their arms and leans back. You:

options.text: Carry on. Body language is often misread
Pivot to a different angle to try to re-engage them
Slow your pace and check in: "Am I tracking with what matters to you?"
Recalibrate based on what topic seemed to shift their posture
Name what you're noticing: "I get the sense something just landed differently than I intended."

questions.prompt: A prospect tells you they have "no budget" for what you're proposing. Most often this signals:

options.text: Exactly what they said. The budget doesn't exist
They want to see how you respond under financial pressure
Budget exists, but they haven't yet bought into the value
Budget could be found if the priority were higher
Budget exists somewhere, but they don't have the authority to release it

questions.prompt: You're in a meeting with three stakeholders. The most senior person says nothing the entire time. You read this as:

options.text: A sign their role here is mainly to listen and observe
Trust in their team to lead the conversation
Active assessment of how their team interacts with you
Possible disengagement worth checking on later
They're the real decision-maker, and the room is performing for them

questions.prompt: A normally warm contact is noticeably curt with you today. Your approach for the rest of the call:

options.text: Match their energy so you're not thrown off your agenda
Push through your planned agenda as normal
Soften your tone and go gently for the rest of the call
Ask a light, low-pressure check-in before continuing
Name it plainly: "You seem a bit different today, everything okay on your end?"

questions.prompt: You're presenting to a technical buyer and a commercial buyer at once. The technical buyer is nodding; the commercial buyer looks unconvinced. You:

options.text: Keep the pitch as planned since one of them is clearly on side
Address the commercial buyer's likely concerns generically before moving on
Ask the commercial buyer directly what would need to be true for this to work for them
Split your attention evenly between both for the rest of the meeting
Name the gap: "I can see this is landing differently for each of you. Let's talk about that."

questions.prompt: A prospect says they're "excited" about your proposal but their body language and pace say otherwise. You:

options.text: Take the word at face value and move to next steps
Slow down and ask a broader open question about their priorities
Repeat the benefits in case they missed something
Ask what would need to happen internally for this to move forward
Name the mismatch gently: "You say excited, but something in the room feels more cautious. What's the caution about?"

questions.prompt: A buyer you're negotiating with keeps deferring to a colleague who isn't in the room. You:

options.text: Keep negotiating with the person in front of you as if they hold full authority
Ask general questions about their internal process
Suggest getting the colleague on a call before going further
Ask what that colleague would need to see to be comfortable
Name the pattern: "You've mentioned them a few times now. What's their actual stake in this decision?"

questions.prompt: In a group demo, one attendee keeps checking their phone while others are engaged. You:

options.text: Ignore it and keep presenting to the engaged majority
Raise your energy to try to win their attention back
Direct a specific, easy question their way to re-engage them
Pause briefly and ask the group if this is still a good use of everyone's time
Note it, and follow up with them individually after to find out what pulled their focus

questions.prompt: Your manager delivers blunt critical feedback in a one-to-one. Your first internal reaction:

options.text: Defensive. You start building counter-arguments in your head
Direct. You push back on the spot to test the reasoning
Measured. You absorb it and decide how to respond later
Curious. You ask questions to understand the concern underneath it
Open. You name what you're feeling: "That stings a bit, give me a second to sit with it."

questions.prompt: A prospect raises their voice at you on a call. You:

options.text: Match their energy to show you're not intimidated
De-escalate by immediately agreeing with whatever they're upset about
Stay quiet, let them finish, then respond calmly
Hold steady and ask a calibrated question to slow the moment down
Name what's happening: "Something's clearly hit a nerve here. Talk me through it."

questions.prompt: A colleague takes public credit for an idea you brought to the team. You:

options.text: Let it slide. The work matters more than the credit
Note it privately and watch for a pattern over time
Raise it with them one-to-one after the meeting
Raise it cleanly in the moment without making it personal
Name it directly: "That was actually my idea. I'd like the next one to land properly."

questions.prompt: A client has cancelled on you three times in a row. Internally you feel:

options.text: Anxious that the deal is slipping away
Frustrated, and you start to question whether they're worth chasing
Curious about what's actually going on for them
Pragmatic. The pattern itself is data worth acting on
Direct. Time to name the pattern openly rather than reschedule again

questions.prompt: You're three weeks into a slump with no closes. Your dominant self-talk is:

options.text: "Push harder. More activity will fix this."
"Slumps end. Just keep showing up."
"Time to ask for a fresh set of eyes on my pipeline."
"What am I missing? What's the pattern in the losses?"
"The pressure I'm under is itself changing how I'm showing up right now."

questions.prompt: Your manager hands you a difficult account known for burning out reps. You:

options.text: Accept it and quietly wonder if you're being set up to fail
Take it as a chance to prove yourself
Approach it as a learning opportunity regardless of outcome
Spend time understanding what previous reps got wrong first
Ask your manager directly what success looks like and what support is on offer

questions.prompt: A client who was warm has gone completely quiet for over a week. Your gut says:

options.text: They're probably just busy, keep following up on a normal schedule
They have some hesitation but aren't ready to raise it yet
Something changed internally, worth reaching out to find out what
Someone else may hold sway and hasn't been convinced yet
Name it directly in your next message: "I sense something's shifted, what's changed since we last spoke?"

questions.prompt: It's three days from the end of the period and you're well short of target. Your default move:

options.text: High activity. More calls, more emails, work the pipe hard
Step back for an hour to think strategically before acting
Triage the pipeline and focus only on what can realistically close
Lean on your strongest relationships with a direct, honest ask
Pick up the phone to your best contacts and ask plainly for the business

questions.prompt: A procurement contact says: "Match this price or we go with the other vendor." You:

options.text: Match the price straight away to protect the relationship
Defend your price firmly using feature and value comparisons
Ask for time to consult your manager before responding
Acknowledge the pressure they're under and ask what outcome they're really trying to protect
Name the pressure directly and ask what success actually looks like for them here

questions.prompt: Mid-demo, the software crashes in front of the whole buying committee. You:

options.text: Apologise and try to reboot as quickly as possible
Acknowledge the failure, lighten the room, and switch to a backup explanation
Stay composed and suggest reconvening once it's working again
Use the dead time to deepen discovery instead
Name it openly: "Not the demo gods' finest hour. Here's exactly what you would have seen."

questions.prompt: A prospect blindsides you with a technical question you genuinely can't answer. You:

options.text: Attempt an answer and risk being wrong
Buy time with "great question" while you think of something
Redirect: "Before I answer, help me understand why that matters for you."
Commit to a precise answer within a clear timeframe
Say honestly: "I don't know. I'll find out and have it to you today."

questions.prompt: A senior person is openly sceptical in a meeting and the rest of the room goes quiet. You:

options.text: Try to win them over by agreeing with their concerns
Push back directly: "I think we see this differently, can we work through it?"
Hold your position politely and let the evidence speak
Slow the conversation down and ask what's actually behind the concern
Name it: "This isn't landing the way I'd hoped. What would be useful to dig into?"

questions.prompt: A senior buyer sets a hard deadline: "Final answer by Friday, or we go with someone else." You:

options.text: Move quickly to accommodate the deadline and secure the deal
Confirm the deadline and adjust your process to meet it
Hold steady, explain your process, and propose a realistic counter-timeline
Acknowledge the timeline and ask what's actually driving the urgency
Name what's underneath it: "Before I respond to the deadline, help me understand what's actually changed since we last spoke."

questions.prompt: The most effective opening in the first 60 seconds with a brand new prospect:

options.text: A clear summary of who you are and what you do
A provocative question that challenges their current thinking
A specific story about a similar client and the problem you solved for them
A direct question about a pressure point you already suspect they're feeling
A relevant insight about their situation that earns you the next five minutes

questions.prompt: Explaining a technically complex feature to a non-technical buyer, you:

options.text: Walk them through it step by step at a simplified level
Hand it to a technical colleague and stay focused on the commercial picture
Skip the mechanics and focus only on the business outcome
Use an analogy from a world they already understand
Tell a short story about a customer who had the same gap and what changed for them

questions.prompt: The strongest follow-up message after receiving a no:

options.text: A polite thank-you and a request to stay in touch
An article or insight relevant to the reason they declined
A direct question: "Help me understand what would need to be different next time."
A reflection of what you've learned that might be useful to them regardless
A short story about a buyer who once said no, came back later, and what changed

questions.prompt: You're the third vendor the prospect has spoken to this month, and they've heard versions of your pitch twice already. You:

options.text: Differentiate on price or commercial terms
Differentiate on service, support, or relationship
Reframe the actual problem you think you're solving
Lead with a story or insight the other two are unlikely to have shared
Name the situation: "You've heard versions of this twice already. Here's what I think the others missed."

questions.prompt: A prospect pushes back hard on your pricing. The strongest response:

options.text: Hold the price and explain that quality has a cost
Walk them through the value calculation logically
Ask what they're comparing it to, and explore the gap
Tell the story of a buyer who picked the cheaper option and what that choice cost them
Reframe what's actually being decided: "This isn't really about price, is it?"

questions.prompt: The most powerful version of a customer case study in a pitch centres on:

options.text: The numbers and metrics: percentage improvements, dollar impact
The specific moment the customer realised they had the problem
The before-and-after transformation of the customer's situation
The decision moment when the customer chose to act
The human behind the result: who they were, what they feared, what changed

questions.prompt: EQ Identity EQ1

options.text: When a prospect is emotional, my strength is staying calm and not reacting
My strength is using their emotion as information that tells me what to do next
My strength is noticing the emotion before they've said anything about it
My strength is naming the emotion out loud, even when it's uncomfortable

questions.prompt: EQ Identity EQ2

options.text: In a tense negotiation, I'm the one who keeps the room steady
I'm quick to sense a shift in energy and move before anyone else reacts
I pick up on what's not being said faster than most people in the room
I'll say the thing everyone else is thinking but avoiding out loud

questions.prompt: EQ Identity EQ3

options.text: My default under pressure is composure. I don't let the moment rattle me
My default under pressure is momentum. I use the tension to move things forward
My default under pressure is attention. I slow down and watch closely before acting
My default under pressure is honesty. I say plainly what I think is happening
